title: The blow and the flight
hookLine: the grown Musa strikes a man who dies, repents at once, and flees Egypt

lines: THE SECOND YOU CAN'T TAKE BACK.
cards: Everyone has a moment they'd give anything to take back. The angry text. The slammed door.
It took a second, and it's lasted years. The baby from the river is a grown man now, given wisdom and knowledge, the Qur'an says.
One day he walks into the city at an hour when nobody's paying attention, and finds two men fighting, one from his own people, one from Pharaoh's side. His man shouts for help.
Musa steps in and strikes the other man, once. And the man falls, and doesn't get up.

teach.b: Look how fast Musa turns. In Surah al-Qasas, his words come right there over the body. First: this is of Satan's doing; he is an enemy, a clear misleader.
Then, straight to Allah: my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.
And the next words: so He forgave him. He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Two sentences.
No excuses about the fight, or who started it, or that he was only defending someone. The Arabic is zalamtu nafsi: I wronged my own self.
In the Qur'an's way of seeing it, when you do wrong, the first person you injure is you.
Muslim scholars generally explain that Musa never meant to kill; the word for the blow suggests a punch, a single strike with the fist. But he doesn't hide behind that.
Then a promise: my Lord, because of the favor You've shown me, I will never be a helper to the guilty. The very next day, he's tested. The same man is fighting again, calling to him again.
As Musa moves toward the other man, a voice cries out: Musa, do you mean to kill me, the way you killed a man yesterday?
Then a man comes running from the far end of the city: the chiefs are plotting to kill you. Get out.

I'm giving you good advice. And Musa leaves Egypt, afraid, watching over his shoulder, praying: my Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people. The prince of the palace walks into the desert with nothing.
The Qur'an doesn't hide its prophets' worst moments. It shows what they did with them.

how: Muslims seek forgiveness with istighfar, asking Allah's pardon, often many times a day, and Musa's words "my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me" are among the Qur'anic prayers people use.

o: I defended myself in a fight
I have wronged my own self
I have been wronged by others

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a single strike, not meant to kill
the chiefs are plotting: get out

s: Musa made excuses for the killing
he said at once: my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.
the Qur'an says Allah forgave him
right after his prayer: so He forgave him. He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
Musa left Egypt calm and unafraid
he left afraid, watching over his shoulder, praying to be saved from the wrongdoing people.

games.q: you're Musa. you've struck a man once and he's dead. you never meant it. what do you say first?
o: he started it. I was defending someone.
my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.
games.why: he names it as Satan's doing and then turns straight to Allah: I have wronged myself, forgive me. the Qur'an says: so He forgave him.

practice: Let one moment come up, a small one is fine, when anger moved faster than you did; don't replay the argument or build the case for why you were right. Just see it, and say inside the plain version: I did that.
If you pray, you can use Musa's words, my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me; if you don't, simply own it for a while without an excuse.

wordCard.voice: Zalamtu nafsi: I have wronged my own self. What Musa said over the body, before he even asked for forgiveness.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:16: "I have wronged my own self."

carryVoice: Your line: my lord, I wronged myself. The short kind, no excuses attached. That's day forty-six.
